mentions.author: abeppu
mentions.story: Deriving Dependently-Typed OOP from First Principles
mentions.text:
Maybe I'm just missing something, but I'm not on board with the definitions they take in the introduction.

> the essence of object-oriented programming is programming against interfaces, which correspond to the type theoretic concept of codata and copattern matching

They then use the classic codata example of a Stream, with a head and a tail. The Stream they declare looks a lot more like the version of that concept in functional languages than the version of it in an OO one, but clearly it exists in both paradigms.

mentions.author: defanor
mentions.story: You might as well timestamp it
mentions.text:
As mentioned in other comments, there's a bunch of drawbacks with this approach, but there's a more general term "boolean blindness" [1], which is usually applied to programs (not databases). I find it useful to avoid using booleans where more descriptive types make sense (and can be used), as well as not throwing information away when it may be needed still, but to a reasonable extent.

mentions.author: rpearl
mentions.story: SICP is being taught again at MIT
mentions.text:
CMU doesn't have any course explicitly on Haskell. There is a freshman course on functional programming, which is taught in Standard ML and therefore definitely has a focus on the advantages of an expressive type system.( [course]).

There are multiple other courses where a functional paradigm is either necessary or very useful as well ( [course], [course], [course], [link], among others).

There are currently no courses which teach object-oriented programming.

mentions.author: _delirium
mentions.story: Simon Peyton-Jones - A Taste of Haskell
mentions.text:
Do you know why ML won out at CMU?

As far as research goes, CMU and Princeton are (as far as I know) the two ML strongholds in the US, with functional-programming research at most other departments dominated by Haskell. So I imagine the faculty were in favor of ML. The new course ( [course]) is being taught by Robert Harper, author of the book Programming in Standard ML ( [course]).
